intro:
In 1992 a Macintosh shareware author decided that Asteroids deserved better, and spent an unreasonable amount of effort proving it. Maelstrom has rendered 3D rock sprites, a proper soundtrack, screen-shaking explosions, power-ups, and a sense of weight that the 1979 original never had. It is still, more than thirty years on, one of the best arcade games written for any Macintosh.

It boots straight into the game here, with nothing to install. Ambrosia later released the engine under the GPL and the artwork under Creative Commons, which is why it can be here at all — though the 1990s build you are playing still opens with the shareware notice it shipped with. Click Not Yet and play.

Maelstrom's own Preferences dialog lists every key and lets you change them, which is worth doing if the defaults fight your keyboard.

sections.h: What makes it more than a clone
sections.html:
The rocks are the giveaway. They are not vector outlines or flat polygons; they are pre-rendered 3D objects, tumbling in animation frames, and in 1992 on a Macintosh that was showing off. Shoot one and it breaks into smaller ones that are also properly rendered, and the screen jolts.

On top of that sits everything Asteroids did not have. Power-ups drift down and change your ship: multiple shots, autofire, shields, extra lives. Enemy ships arrive and actually aim. There are bonus levels. There is a two-player mode over AppleTalk, which is not much use here. And there is a high score table that Ambrosia ran as a genuine worldwide contest, which is the sort of thing a shareware author did when the alternative was nothing.

It is also hard in the way arcade games were hard: not unfair, but not interested in whether you are having a nice time.

sections.h: Why this game matters beyond the Mac
sections.html:
Maelstrom is the reason SDL exists.

In 1995 Ambrosia gave the source to Sam Lantinga, who wanted to port it to Linux. The cross-platform layer he wrote to do that became the Simple DirectMedia Layer — the library that now underpins an enormous amount of game development, from indie projects to the Steam client and countless commercial ports. It started as scaffolding to get a Macintosh Asteroids game running on X11.

Ambrosia Software itself was one of the great shareware houses: Maelstrom, Escape Velocity, Apeiron, SketchFighter, and a registration system built on trust and good jokes. You can still see that model working in the notice this build opens with — pay if you keep playing, on your honour. The company wound down in the 2010s, but Maelstrom was set free first: GPL for the code in 1999, Creative Commons for the art in 2010.

If you want to play it at a modern resolution on a modern machine, the SDL port is maintained and packaged nearly everywhere. What is here is the 1990s Macintosh build, in its own habitat.

faq.q: The game says Maelstrom is not a free product. Should it be here?
faq.a: Yes, and by Ambrosia's own rules. That notice is the shareware pitch it shipped with in the 1990s: try it, and pay if you keep playing. Shareware was built to be passed around, and the licence file on this disk says non-profit distribution is acceptable without asking, so long as nothing is modified and the complete package is included. Both conditions hold here — the notice is deliberately left intact rather than patched out. Ambrosia also released the engine under the GPL in 1999 and the artwork under Creative Commons in 2010.

faq.q: Is it legal to have this here?
faq.a: Yes. The engine is GPL and the artwork is Creative Commons Attribution, both by the decision of the people who made them. That is a firmer footing than most things preserved from this era, which survive only because nobody is left to object.

faq.q: Do I need to install anything?
faq.a: No. The emulator is WebAssembly and runs in this page. Nothing is installed and nothing is uploaded.

faq.q: What is the connection to SDL?
faq.a: Sam Lantinga wrote the Simple DirectMedia Layer while porting Maelstrom from the Mac to Linux in the mid-1990s. SDL went on to become one of the most widely used game libraries there is.

intro:
Nobody had asked for a game with no way to win. Will Wright built a city editor as a tool for another project, noticed he enjoyed the tool more than the project, and spent four years failing to convince a publisher that a toy about zoning and tax rates was worth selling. Maxis released it in 1989 and it created a genre.

This is that original, on the Macintosh, in black and white. No 3D, no tutorial, no advisors — a grid, three zone types, and a budget you will get wrong.

This is the original, so a lot of what modern players expect is absent. There are no advisors telling you what is wrong, no tutorial, and no undo. The manual did the teaching, and the game assumed you would read it.

sections.h: The whole game, in three zones
sections.html:
You paint three kinds of zone — residential, commercial, industrial — connect them with roads and power, and then watch what happens. Nothing grows unless it has power and a road. Industry pollutes and residents move away from pollution. Commerce needs residents to shop and workers to staff it. Raise taxes and growth slows; lower them and you cannot pay for the fire service, which matters more than it sounds.

That is the entire model, and it is enough to produce a city that surprises you. The famous part is that there is no win condition. You are not beating anything. You are running a place, and the only judgement is whether it works.

There are also disasters — fires, floods, tornadoes, and a monster — which exist mostly so that the simulation has something to recover from.

sections.h: Why it took four years to publish
sections.html:
Wright built the city editor for Raid on Bungeling Bay, a 1984 Commodore 64 shooter, and found that laying out the cities was more interesting than bombing them. The game that resulted had no score, no opponent and no ending, and every publisher he showed it to explained that this was not a game.

Jeff Braun disagreed, and the two of them founded Maxis to publish it. SimCity came out in 1989 for the Macintosh and the Amiga, sold slowly, won awards, and then sold for a decade. It produced SimEarth, SimAnt, SimTower, The Sims — which became the best-selling PC game series ever made — and an entire category of software about running a system rather than defeating one.

In 2008 EA released the original engine as open source under the GPL, renamed Micropolis, for the One Laptop Per Child project. The code behind this game is free software; the name is not.

faq.q: Is this the real original SimCity?
faq.a: Yes — version 1.2 of the 1989 Macintosh release, in black and white, running as it shipped. Not SimCity Classic for Windows, not the 1993 SNES version, and not any of the remakes.

faq.q: Why is it black and white?
faq.a: The Macintosh original was. Colour Macs existed by 1989 but the game targeted the compact machines most people owned, and the whole visual design is built from dither patterns.

faq.q: Why a Macintosh SE and not something faster?
faq.a: Because this build will not run on anything else. It is the black-and-white release, and it refuses to start on a colour screen — it opens, finds a colour monitor, and quits. The SE gives it the 512×342 one-bit display it was written for.

Begin a new city, choose a terrain, then lay a road, place a power plant, and zone a small residential area near it. Nothing grows without both power and road access, which is the first thing everyone gets wrong.

faq.q: There is no tutorial. Is that right?
faq.a: That is right. The game shipped with a printed manual that did the teaching, and it assumes you will experiment. Keep the first city small and watch what the budget does.

Arashi does the same, on a Macintosh, in 1993, with colour, a soundtrack and a level compiler its authors wrote so the game could be scripted. sections.h: What it added to Tempest
sections.html:
The shape is familiar: you run around the edge of a well, firing down it, while things climb up towards you. Let one reach the rim and it comes for you along it.

What Arashi adds is a decade of hardware. The wells are drawn in colour with proper shading rather than vectors. There is a soundtrack. There are power-ups, a save system, and what the ReadMe calls doomsday levels — the difficulty past the point where the game stops being reasonable.

The most interesting addition is invisible while you play. Juri Munkki wrote a game compiler and scripting language for the 1.1 release, so the levels are data rather than code. That is why the C source shipped alongside the game: the authors expected people to look.

sections.h: Mac shareware as a culture
sections.html:
Arashi is a good example of a category that barely exists now. Two people wrote an arcade game to a standard that would have been commercial a few years earlier, put it on the Info-Mac archive, asked for nothing, and included the source.

The distribution model made that normal. A shareware author had no publisher, no shelf space and no marketing, so the software had to travel by being copied — which meant the licence had to permit copying, and most of them did, in a sentence written by the author rather than a lawyer. Arashi's is one line long.

That is why a site like this can exist at all. A large part of the Macintosh catalogue between 1985 and 2000 was released on terms that explicitly allow what you are doing right now.

author: John Calhoun / Soft Dorothy Software

intro:
You ride an ostrich. So does everyone else, except the ones riding buzzards, and the way you beat them is to be slightly higher than they are at the moment you collide. That is Joust, and Glypha is Joust rebuilt for the Macintosh by John Calhoun — the same person who wrote Glider — with Egyptian tomb art, a sphinx that spits, and a hand that comes out of the lava to take you if you linger.

It is freeware, the source is published, and it boots straight into the game here.

sections.h: The one rule that matters
sections.html:
When two riders collide, the higher one wins. That is the whole combat system, and everything else follows from it: you spend the game trying to arrive at a fight from above, and your opponents are trying to do the same.

Flapping is a tap, not a hold. Each press gives one beat of lift, so altitude is something you build and spend rather than something you steer to. Players who hold the key fly into the ceiling and drop.

Kill an enemy and it leaves an egg. Collect it quickly or it hatches into a fresh rider, which is the pressure that stops the game becoming a stalemate. Wait too long anywhere and the hand comes out of the lava at the bottom of the screen, which is Calhoun's addition and is exactly as alarming as it sounds.

sections.h: Calhoun's other game
sections.html:
John Calhoun is best known for Glider, the paper aeroplane game that ran through four versions between 1988 and 1994 and was published commercially by Casady & Greene. Glypha is the other one: a Joust tribute he wrote for himself, gave away, and eventually published the source to.

Both are unmistakably his. The art is hand-drawn and slightly wry, the physics have weight, and the difficulty is set by someone who expected you to practise. He put the sources for most of his Macintosh work on GitHub under the softdorothy account, which is why ports keep appearing — kainjow/Glypha rebuilds this one for modern systems.

It is air hockey. You are in a bar somewhere off the main sequence, and the person across the table from you is a lizard, or a robot, or a large hairy thing with a grudge. You win, someone else sits down, and they are better than the last one.

Shufflepuck Café came out in 1988 and is one of the handful of games that defined what a Macintosh game looked like: black and white, beautifully drawn, mechanically tiny, and far more characterful than it had any need to be.

sections.h: The opponents are the game
sections.html:
Mechanically there is almost nothing here: a table, two paddles, a puck, and a mouse. What makes it memorable is the bar.

Each opponent is a hand-drawn character with their own way of playing and their own reaction to losing, and they get steadily harder as you work along the line. Some cheat. Some sulk. The artwork is the best argument for one-bit graphics anyone made in the late 1980s — every character is built from dithered black and white and every one of them has a face you remember.

The difficulty curve is steep and the final opponents are genuinely hard, which in 1988 was the point: the game was small enough to fit on a floppy and had to stay interesting for months.

sections.h: Brøderbund, and where this came from
sections.html:
Brøderbund published it — the same company behind Myst, The Print Shop, Where in the World is Carmen Sandiego and Kid Pix. In 1988 they were at their peak, and Shufflepuck Café is a good example of what they did well: take one idea, execute it beautifully, and let the art carry it.

The copy preserved here is a 4am crack, which matters practically rather than morally. The original shipped with copy protection that expected a real floppy drive reading a real disk, so an unmodified image simply will not run in an emulator. Removing that is what makes preservation possible at all.

intro:
Almost everyone who sat in front of a school Macintosh in the 1990s played this. Not the Apple II green-screen original, and not the phone remake — this one, with the drawn title screen, the general store at Independence, and the river you were never sure whether to ford.

It is MECC's Macintosh release, and it runs here on an emulated Mac. You pick a profession, buy supplies with money you will immediately regret spending, and set out in April with five people in a wagon.
launchNote: Boots straight to the title screen on an emulated Macintosh II. Click Travel the Trail, choose a profession — banker is easy, farmer is hard and scores triple — and buy supplies before you leave.

SystemSystem 7.5.3
EmulatorMini vMac, compiled to WebAssembly
VersionThe MECC Macintosh release

This is the Macintosh build, so the art is the detailed pen-and-ink work the Mac version is known for rather than the blocky Apple II graphics. It uses a small palette — the title screen is essentially two-tone on parchment — which is what the machines of the day could manage and what the artists drew for.

Everything is mouse-driven. The one thing worth knowing before you start is that the game does not warn you when you are making the decision that kills you; it just quietly notes it and lets you find out three weeks later.

sections.h: How not to die immediately
sections.html:
Leave in April or May. Leave in March and you hit snow in the mountains. Leave in July and you hit snow in the mountains.

Buy more oxen than you think you need. A dead ox is a stopped wagon, and a stopped wagon in October is the end of the run. Two spare yoke is not excessive.

Do not shoot more than you can carry. Hunting is the most fun part of the game and the easiest way to waste a day: you can only haul a few hundred pounds back to the wagon, and everything else rots where it fell.

Slow the pace and raise the rations when people get sick. Grueling pace plus bare-bones rations is how a party of five becomes a party of one, and the game will let you do it all the way to the end.

Ford only shallow water. Under two and a half feet, ford it. Deeper than that, take the ferry or hire the guide and pay the money. Everyone learns this once, expensively.

sections.h: Why this version is the one people remember
sections.html:
The Oregon Trail started in 1971 as a text program written by three student teachers in Minnesota, typed into a mainframe and played over a teletype. MECC — the Minnesota Educational Computing Consortium — spent the next two decades rebuilding it for each new machine that arrived in schools.

The Apple II version is the one with the historical claim; it is what put the game in classrooms in the first place. But the Macintosh release is the one most people picture, because it is what the school computer labs of the 1990s actually had, and because it is the first version that looked drawn rather than plotted.

It is also a genuinely unusual piece of educational software: it teaches by killing you. There is no quiz and no score screen explaining what you should have learned. There is a long journey, a set of resources, and a river.

faq.q: Is this the version I played at school?
faq.a: If you were on a Macintosh, almost certainly. This is MECC's Macintosh release — the drawn artwork, the mouse-driven store, the ford-or-ferry decision. The Apple II original looks quite different.

faq.q: Do I need to install anything?
faq.a: No. The emulated Mac and the disk both load in the page. There is nothing to download and no plugin.

faq.q: Why do I keep dying of dysentery?
faq.a: Bad water and a hard pace. Slow down, raise the rations, and rest when someone falls ill. The game is happy to let you push a sick party until nobody is left.

faq.q: Should I ford the river or take the ferry?
faq.a: Ford it if the depth is under about two and a half feet. Deeper than that and you are gambling your oxen, your supplies and usually a person against the cost of the ferry.
Banker starts rich and scores single points. Carpenter is the middle. Farmer starts poor, scores triple, and is the one to pick once you have finished the trail at least once.

faq.q: Will my game be saved if I close the tab?
faq.a: Saves live inside the emulated Mac, in your own browser. They survive closing the tab but not clearing site data, and they do not follow you to another device.

faq.q: Can I play it on a phone?
faq.a: It will load, but the game expects a mouse and a keyboard for hunting, so a desktop or laptop is much better.

intro:
Before Halo, Bungie was a small Chicago company making games only for the Macintosh, and Marathon is the one that made their name. It came out in December 1994, six months after Doom shipped on DOS, and it did several things Doom did not: you could look up and down, the levels had real architecture, and — unusually for a shooter in 1994 — it had a plot worth reading.

Bungie put the whole trilogy into free redistribution in 2005, so there is nothing grey about playing it: the entire game is legally free to download. It is not hosted on this site, but the loader below will run your copy on an emulated Macintosh, and the links further down say where to get one.

On a phone it runs, but not at a framerate you would choose to fight in. Reduce the window size inside the game (the plus and minus keys) if it feels heavy.

sections.h: What Marathon actually is
sections.html:
You are a security officer aboard the UESC Marathon, a colony ship built out of the hollowed-out Martian moon Deimos, in orbit around Tau Ceti IV. An alien slave empire called the Pfhor attacks. That is the last simple sentence available about the plot.

What makes Marathon different is that the story is told through computer terminals scattered through the levels, and the three shipboard AIs talking to you through them do not agree with each other. Leela is helpful and straightforward. Durandal is rampant — a technical term in the game's fiction for an AI that has gone through anger and despair and out the other side into something like megalomania — and he is funny, unreliable, and by a distance the most memorable character in a 1994 shooter. Tycho is a third thing entirely.

Mechanically it holds up better than most of its generation. There is real verticality, oxygen management in vacuum levels, friendly BOBs you can accidentally shoot, dual-wielded pistols, and a physics model the community was modifying within months of release.

sections.h: The trilogy, and where to go next
sections.html:
Marathon (1994) was followed by Marathon 2: Durandal in 1995 — which added liquid you could swim in, better level design and a Windows 95 port, the first Bungie game most PC owners saw — and Marathon Infinity in 1996, which shipped with the level editor and a story that deliberately fractures.

All three are free. If you want them at a modern resolution with mouselook, the community engine Aleph One is the way: it is open source, actively maintained, and runs on everything. What you get here instead is the 1994 experience exactly as it shipped, keyboard turning and all.

And the lineage is not subtle. Read Durandal's terminals, then think about Cortana.

faq.a: Yes, and not in a wink-wink way. Bungie authorised free redistribution of the entire Marathon trilogy in 2005, has acknowledged the community's distribution of it repeatedly since, and the trilogy was published free on Steam in 2024 with Bungie's blessing.

faq.q: Is this the full game or a demo?
faq.a: The full game. All of Marathon, every level, not a shareware chapter.

faq.q: Why can't I look up and down with the mouse?
faq.a: Because it is 1994. Marathon does support mouse aiming, but the default configuration is keyboard turning, which is what most people used at the time. If you want modern controls, the Aleph One engine is the better route — it is linked below.

Same studio, and the connections are deliberate. The rampant AI Durandal is the clear ancestor of Cortana, several weapons and ideas carry over, and Bungie has always treated them as part of one lineage. Marathon is not set in the Halo universe, but it is unmistakably the same people.

faq.q: It runs slowly. What can I do?
faq.a: Shrink the game window with the minus key inside Marathon — it renders fewer pixels and the framerate jumps. Close other tabs. And use a desktop or laptop if you can: this is the heaviest title on the site.
At the pattern buffers — the glowing terminal-like devices inside levels. Marathon does not let you save anywhere you like, which takes some getting used to.

Born On Board — the civilian crew. They follow you, they shoot at the Pfhor, they are not very good at it, and they will absolutely walk into your line of fire. Shooting too many of them has consequences.

intro:
Craig Hickman wrote Kid Pix because he watched his three-year-old son try to use MacPaint and fail. Everything in MacPaint punished a mistake; nothing in it made a noise. So he built a drawing program where every tool was obvious, every action made a sound, and nothing you did could be wrong.

This page is about version 1.0 from 1989 — the one Hickman gave away himself, before Brøderbund published it commercially. It is black and white and it was built for a Macintosh Plus, which is a tiny machine: 512 by 342 pixels, and an emulated one starts almost instantly. Bring a copy and the loader below will run it.

A Mac Plus is a tiny machine by any modern measure — eight megahertz, one megabyte of RAM as standard — which is why this is the lightest emulation on the site. It is also why the screen is black and white and rather small. That is not a limitation of the emulator; that was the computer.

sections.h: The tools worth finding
sections.html:
Kid Pix's design principle was that a child should be able to discover everything by poking at it, so the descriptions below are slightly against the spirit of the thing. Poke at it first.

  • The Wacky Brush. Not one brush — a menu of them. Bubbles, dripping paint, a trail of little shapes, echoes of whatever you last drew.
  • The stick of dynamite. One of the erasers. It blows the whole picture up, with a bang.
  • The rubber stamps. A tray of small black-and-white icons — animals, vehicles, faces — that you stamp anywhere.
  • The Electric Mixer. Takes whatever is on the page and scrambles it, in one of several increasingly alarming ways.
  • The letter stamps. Type and each letter arrives with a sound.

Everything makes a noise. The pencil squeaks, the paint can splats, the eraser goes whoosh. Hickman recorded a lot of these himself.

sections.h: What happened next
sections.html:
Brøderbund published Kid Pix commercially in 1991 and it became one of the best-selling pieces of educational software of the decade. Kid Pix Companion followed in 1992 with the slideshow feature, then Kid Pix 2 in 1994 brought colour, and the line continued under Brøderbund, The Learning Company and Riverdeep for years afterwards.

The version here is the one before all of that: Hickman's own release, black and white, with the sounds he recorded and the tools he chose. Plenty of people who loved Kid Pix as children have never seen it. It holds up remarkably well, partly because a program built so that a three-year-old cannot get it wrong turns out to be a pleasant thing for an adult too.

faq.q: Is this the Kid Pix I remember?
faq.a: If you remember colour, it is not — you are remembering Kid Pix 2 from 1994 or later. This is the original 1989 black-and-white version, which is the direct ancestor: same tools, same sounds, same dynamite.
Yes. Craig Hickman released version 1.0 himself as non-commercial software before Brøderbund published the commercial version. The later Brøderbund releases are not hosted here.

faq.q: Why is it black and white?
faq.a: Because the Macintosh Plus it was written for was black and white. Colour Macs existed in 1989 but were expensive, and Kid Pix was built to run on the cheap machine a school or a family actually had.

faq.q: Can I save or print my picture?
faq.a: You can save it inside the emulated Mac and it will still be there next time. Getting it out to a real file on your computer is not wired up yet — it is on the list.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone or tablet?
faq.a: Yes, and better than most things here. The emulated machine is small and simple, and drawing with a finger turns out to suit it.

Craig Hickman, an art professor at the University of Oregon, who wrote it for his son Ben after watching him struggle with MacPaint. He has said the core idea was that a drawing program for a small child should have no wrong moves.

intro:
In 1989 Berkeley Systems shipped a utility that stopped your monitor from burning an image into its phosphor. In 1991 they added a module in which chrome toasters with flapping wings fly slowly across the screen accompanied by slices of toast, and that module became one of the most recognisable pieces of software of the decade.

There are dozens of Flying Toasters tributes on the web built out of CSS and JavaScript. This is not one of them. It is the actual software, on an emulated Macintosh running System 7.5.3, with the control panel, the sliders, and all seventy-one modules Berkeley Systems shipped.

After Dark was not an application — it was a system extension and a control panel, which is why it needs a whole Macintosh around it rather than being something you could port to a web page. That is also why running it means booting System 7 first.

It behaves exactly as it did on a real machine: leave the Mac idle for about a minute and the screensaver takes over. If you would rather not wait, open the control panel from the Apple menu and press Demo.

sections.h: The modules worth your time
sections.html:
• Flying Toasters. The famous one. Chrome toasters, flapping wings, slices of toast, and a slider for how many.
  • Fish! An aquarium. Berkeley Systems' first hit module and, for a lot of offices, the reason After Dark got bought.
  • Mowin' Man. A small man mows your screen. When he finishes, it grows back.
  • Warp. Stars streaking past. Simple, and the one that looked best on a big monitor.
  • Boris. A cat that walks across your screen, and later got a whole product to himself.
  • Rainstorm. Rain down the glass with thunder. Genuinely calming, thirty-five years on.

There is also a Randomizer, which cycles modules, and a MultiModule that runs several at once — which on a 1991 Macintosh was showing off.

sections.h: Why a screensaver mattered
sections.html:
The original justification was technical and real. Cathode-ray tubes with a static image left on them for weeks would retain a ghost of it permanently, and in an office full of terminals showing the same spreadsheet all day, that was a genuine hardware problem.

What Berkeley Systems worked out is that the fix could be entertainment. A screensaver is a piece of software with no job to do and complete freedom over the screen, running in an era when almost every other program was a grid of grey boxes. After Dark was one of the first pieces of software people bought for pleasure rather than for a task, and the toasters ended up on t-shirts, mugs and a lawsuit with Jefferson Airplane over whose flying toasters came first.

LCD panels do not burn in the way CRTs did, so the technical reason evaporated. The toasters outlived it comfortably.

faq.q: How do I make the toasters appear?
faq.a: Either wait or skip the wait. Left alone for about a minute the emulated Mac goes idle and After Dark starts on its own, which is what it did on a real machine. To choose a module yourself, open Apple menu › Control Panels › After Dark, pick one from the list on the left, and press Demo.

faq.q: Is this the real After Dark or a web imitation?
faq.a: The real software. There are many Flying Toasters tributes built in CSS, JavaScript or as modern screensavers; this is Berkeley Systems' actual Macintosh release running inside an emulated Macintosh, control panel and all.
The Macintosh After Dark from the early 1990s, the version whose module set includes Flying Toasters, Fish!, Mowin' Man, Warp and Boris.

faq.q: Why does it need a whole emulated Macintosh?
faq.a: Because After Dark was a system extension, not an application. It hooked into the Mac OS to take over the screen when the machine went idle, which means it only exists in the context of a running Mac OS.

It is genuinely murky. Berkeley Systems was acquired in the late 1990s and the After Dark name has changed hands more than once since, but nobody has sold the Macintosh version in decades. If you hold the rights, the takedown page is linked in the footer.

faq.q: Were the Flying Toasters stolen from Jefferson Airplane?
faq.a: Jefferson Airplane sued over it in 1994, pointing at the cover of their 1973 album Thirty Seconds Over Winterland, which has flying toasters on it. The case did not go the band's way.

faq.q: Can I use it as my actual screensaver?
faq.a: No — it runs inside the emulated Mac, in a browser tab, so it has no way to take over your real screen. What you get is the thing itself, on demand.

You are a paper aeroplane. You are indoors. Gravity is pulling you down and the only thing keeping you up is the hot air coming out of the heating vents, so the whole game is a slow negotiation with a house that is full of candles, drips, rubber bands and a cat.

Glider PRO is the 1994 peak of a series John Calhoun had been refining since 1988, and in 2016 he put the whole thing — code and art — on GitHub under the GPL. It is free in every sense, and it boots straight into the Slumberland house here.

If you want Glider PRO at a modern resolution with gamepad support and the level editor, there is a maintained port called Aerofoil built on Calhoun's released source. It is the better way to play seriously. What is here is the original, as it shipped.

sections.h: The house, and everything in it
sections.html:
Each room is a single screen and the glider drifts through it left to right, or right to left, or up through a hole in the ceiling. The furniture is the level design:

  • Heating vents and air ducts. Your engine. Hover over one to climb; the entire skill of the game is learning to ride them.
  • Candles. Fly through the flame and the paper burns. Obviously.
  • Drips and steam. Wet paper does not fly.
  • Rubber bands and paper clips. Fired at you by things that resent your presence.
  • The cat. A problem.
  • Batteries, helium, and the paper aeroplane power-ups. Temporary thrust, temporary lift, and extra lives.

Glider PRO shipped with several houses and a built-in editor, and the community built hundreds more. That editor is the reason the game is still alive: there is far more Glider content made by players than by Casady & Greene.

sections.h: Why it was freed
sections.html:
John Calhoun wrote the first Glider in 1988 as shareware, and the series ran through Glider 3.1.4 and Glider 4.0 before Casady & Greene published Glider PRO commercially in 1994. Casady & Greene closed in 2003.

In 2016 Calhoun put the complete source on GitHub under the GPL — the Macintosh Programmer's Workshop project files, the resource forks, the artwork, everything. That is rarer than it sounds. Most Macintosh games of that era are stuck in limbo because the publisher dissolved and nobody is sure who inherited what. Glider PRO is simply free, because the person who wrote it decided it should be.

faq.q: It asks for 256 colours as soon as it starts. What do I pick?
faq.a: Pick 256. Glider PRO wants colour and offers to switch the screen for you; that dialog is the game's own, exactly as it shipped, and nothing here is patched to remove it. Choosing 16 greys also works and looks closer to how it ran on a cheaper Mac of the period.
Yes, genuinely. John Calhoun released the source code and the game assets on GitHub in 2016 under the GNU GPL version 2.

Get the paper aeroplane through the house to the end without burning, soaking or shredding it. Later houses add doors you have to find keys for and rooms that only open once you have done something elsewhere.

faq.q: How do I stay in the air?
faq.a: Ride the updrafts. The vents and ducts blow upward — position yourself over one and you rise. Most deaths are from trying to cross a room with no lift in it.

faq.q: Can I build my own houses?
faq.a: Glider PRO shipped with a level editor and it is in this version. The modern Aerofoil port has a better one and can import the hundreds of houses the community made.

faq.q: Should I play this or Aerofoil?
faq.a: Aerofoil if you want to play a lot of it — modern resolution, gamepad support, the community houses. This one if you want the 1994 game exactly as it was, in one click, with nothing installed.
Several. Glider 4.0 from 1991 is the direct predecessor and Calhoun released its source too. It is simpler, black and white, and charming in its own right.

sections.h: What changed from Marathon
sections.html:
The obvious addition is liquid. Marathon 2 lets you swim, and it uses that for whole levels of underwater navigation and for lava you have to cross quickly. It sounds small; it changes the shape of the level design completely.

Less obvious but more important: the levels are better. The first Marathon was corridors in a spaceship, which is what 1994 shooters were. Marathon 2 is set on a planet, with outdoor spaces, ruined architecture and rooms that look like places rather than arenas.

There are also allies. The S'pht'Kr fight alongside you, and the game is careful to make you notice when they die. Durandal is still in charge, still rampant, still funnier than a computer in a shooter has any right to be, and considerably more open about the fact that he is using you.

Bungie shipped Marathon 2 for Windows 95 in 1996 under the name Marathon 2: Durandal. It did not sell especially well against Quake, which arrived the same year, but it is the hinge between Bungie the Mac developer and Bungie the studio Microsoft bought in 2000.

It is a 1996 first-person shooter structured like a short story that folds back on itself, and it should not work as well as it does.

sections.h: The branching that is not branching
sections.html:
Infinity presents itself as a story with alternative paths, and the trick is that your choices are not what move you between them — dying is. Fail in particular ways and the game does not simply reload; it continues somewhere else, in a different version of events, sometimes on a different side of the war.

Because of that, the level list is not the story order, and two people who finish Infinity will describe different games. In 1996 this was genuinely novel and there was no walkthrough to spoil it.

It is also the hardest of the three by some distance. If you want the trilogy's best-paced game, that is Marathon 2. Infinity is the one to play afterwards, when you want it to be strange.

Bungie shipped Infinity with its own tools: Forge for building levels and Anvil for editing the sprites, sounds and physics. Nothing else in 1996 handed you the editors the developers had used, and the result was a modding community that produced hundreds of complete total conversions — some of them, like the Eternal and Rubicon projects, larger than the games they were built on.

That community is why all three games still run on modern machines through the Aleph One engine, which grew out of the Marathon 2 source Bungie released in 2000.

There is no colour, no layers, no alpha, and one level of undo. The canvas is a single page the size of a sheet of paper and it does not scroll beyond that.

Those are not omissions. They are the machine: 128K of memory, a 512×342 one-bit screen, and a 400K floppy. What Atkinson did with that is the reason the program is still worth opening.

sections.h: The things in here that you use every day
sections.html:
The lasso selects by shape rather than by rectangle, snapping tight around whatever you drew. Nobody had done that before.

FatBits zooms to individual pixels while showing the full-size image in a corner, so you can edit one pixel and see the result at actual size. Every pixel editor since has some version of this.

The paint bucket — flood fill, bounded by whatever lines you have drawn. Also new.

The patterns along the bottom are how a one-bit program gets greys. There are thirty-eight, and you can edit them, and the entire visual language of 1980s Macintosh graphics comes out of them.

Marching ants, the animated dashes around a selection, were invented here, because Atkinson needed a selection outline that stayed visible against both black and white.

sections.h: Why it mattered so much
sections.html:
MacPaint shipped free with every Macintosh, alongside MacWrite, and the pair did the arguing for the machine. A mouse and a bitmapped screen sound like abstractions until somebody hands you a pencil tool and you draw a line by moving your hand.

Atkinson also wrote QuickDraw, the graphics layer the whole Macintosh was built on, which is why MacPaint could be so fast on hardware that had no business being fast. He is the same person who invented the pull-down menu, the double-click, and later built HyperCard.

In 2010, Apple gave the MacPaint 1.3 source to the Computer History Museum, which published it: around 5,800 lines of Pascal and assembly. It is worth looking at if you ever want to see what one very good programmer could do with 128K.

sections.h: The modes, and which one is hardest
sections.html:
• Multiples. Eat every multiple of the given number. The gentlest mode and the one everyone remembers.
  • Factors. Eat the factors of the given number. Genuinely harder, because it requires you to think in the other direction.
  • Primes. Eat the prime numbers. Fine until the grid fills with numbers in the eighties and nineties.
  • Equality and Inequality. Eat the expressions that equal — or do not equal — the target. The ones that turn a maths drill into a reading-speed test.

sections.h: Why MECC's games worked
sections.html:
The Minnesota Educational Computing Consortium was a state-funded body set up to put computers into Minnesota's schools, and it ended up making some of the most widely played software of the 1980s and 1990s almost by accident. The Oregon Trail is the famous one, but Number Munchers, Word Munchers, Odell Lake and Fraction Munchers were on every lab machine in North America.

What they got right was that the education had to be the mechanic rather than a reward attached to one. You do not answer a maths question to earn a turn at a game; eating the right number is the game, and the Troggle closing in is what makes you answer quickly. That is a harder design problem than it looks, and most educational software since has failed it.

You are a small figure in a lattice of brick and ladders. There is gold on the screen and guards chasing you, and your only weapon is the ability to dig a hole in the floor beside you. A guard falls in. The hole fills back up. You get on with it.

That is the whole game, and Broderbund built 150 levels out of it. This is the Macintosh version, and it includes the level editor that turned a puzzle game into a thing people made things with.

The whole game is on one screen at a time, in black and white, which is all it ever needed. Collect every piece of gold on a level and a ladder appears that takes you to the next one.

Digging is the entire trick. You cannot jump, you cannot fight, and you cannot outrun a guard forever. You can only remove a piece of floor next to you, which a guard will then fall into, and which will heal shut after a few seconds — with the guard inside it if you were fast enough, and with you inside it if you were not.

sections.h: Why it is harder than it looks
sections.html:
Every level is a small logic problem wearing an action game's clothes. The gold is reachable, but usually only in one order, and often only if you have already trapped a guard somewhere useful — a guard standing in a hole is a platform you can run across.

Guards also carry gold. A guard who picks up a piece drops it when he falls, which means some levels cannot be finished without deliberately letting one rob you first. Working that out is the moment the game stops being about reflexes.

The later levels are pure trap design: a wrong dig walls you in permanently, and the game will happily let you stand in a sealed pocket of brick until you give up and restart the level.

sections.h: The editor, and what it started
sections.html:
Lode Runner shipped with a level editor in 1983, which was close to unheard of. Not a hidden debug mode — a documented feature, on the menu, with a save command.

The result was that people made levels and swapped them on disks and over bulletin boards, and a game with 150 levels effectively never ran out. It is one of the earliest mainstream examples of a game treating its own content as something players should be making, which is now such a normal idea that it is strange to point at.

The editor is on the menu bar here, and the levels you build save into the emulated Mac.

faq.a: It is the Macintosh release of it, version 1.0, in black and white with all 150 levels and the editor. Not Lode Runner Legacy or any of the later Tozai remakes, which are new games.
Z and X dig the floor to your left and right. You cannot dig the floor you are standing on, and you cannot dig solid stone — only the brick.

faq.q: I have walled myself in. Now what?
faq.a: Restart the level. The game does not consider this a bug, and the later levels are designed so that a careless dig is fatal.

faq.q: Can I make my own levels?

If you have ever cleared a pile of mahjong tiles by matching free pairs, you have played a copy of this. Shanghai is where that layout came from — not a folk game, not a traditional pastime, but a specific piece of software written by one person in 1986.

This is the Macintosh version, booting from its own floppy, in black and white, with the tile set drawn small enough to fit a compact Mac's screen.

Like Rogue, this one boots from the original disk rather than from a System 7 hard disk, because the 1986 application does not survive System 7.5.3 — it takes the machine down with it. The floppy carries its own System and names Shanghai as the startup program, so the emulated Mac Plus comes up directly in the game.

A tile is free if nothing sits on top of it and at least one of its left or right edges is clear. Click two free tiles that match and they are removed. Clear all 144 and you have won, which happens less often than you would think.

sections.h: Not actually mahjong
sections.html:
Shanghai uses a mahjong tile set and almost nothing else from mahjong. The real game is a four-player game of draws and discards with scoring rules that take a while to learn. What Brodie Lockard built is a solitaire puzzle that happens to use the same 144 tiles.

Lockard based the layout on a design he had read about — the "turtle" arrangement — and wrote the first version on the PLATO system while recovering from a gymnastics accident that had left him almost entirely paralysed. Activision picked it up and published it on the Macintosh in 1986.

It is worth saying plainly because the misunderstanding is so widespread: this is a 1986 computer game with an inventor, not an ancient Chinese pastime. The confusion is itself a measure of how completely it took over.

sections.h: Why it is not always winnable
sections.html:
The tiles are dealt into the layout at random, and the game does not check that the deal can be solved. Some deals cannot be. You can play perfectly and still reach a board with four tiles left where the only pair is stacked on itself.

Later mahjong solitaire games usually guarantee a solvable deal, which makes them fairer and slightly less interesting. Here, part of the skill is reading the board early — clearing the tiles that unlock the most, and being careful about breaking up a set of four when the other two are buried.

faq.a: Yes. Brodie Lockard wrote it, Activision published it in 1986, and every mahjong solitaire game since is a descendant of this layout.

faq.q: Why can I not always win?
faq.a: Because the deal is not checked for solvability. Some boards are dead from the start, which is a genuine property of the original and not a fault in the emulation.

faq.q: Why does it boot straight into the game?
faq.a: The floppy names Shanghai as the startup program rather than the Finder, so the machine comes up in the game. The 1986 application will not run under System 7 at all, so this is also the only way it works.

faq.q: How do I know if a tile is free?
faq.a: Nothing on top of it, and nothing immediately to its left or immediately to its right. A tile with neighbours on both sides is locked even if it is on the top layer.

Everyone who has played a roguelike has played a descendant of this. Rogue invented the whole shape of it in 1980 — a dungeon generated fresh every time, permanent death, and items whose identity you have to work out by using them and finding out.

This one runs differently from most of the catalogue, and the difference is worth explaining. Nearly every title here is copied onto a System 7 hard disk that boots and then launches it. Rogue will not tolerate that — launch it under System 7.5.3 and it takes the whole machine down hard enough that the Mac resets and asks for a startup disk.

It does not need one. The original floppy names Rogue itself as the startup program, where a normal disk names the Finder. There is no desktop, no menu bar you did not ask for, no Finder at all: the machine boots directly into the game, which is exactly what a 1985 Epyx disk did. So that is how it runs here, on a Macintosh Plus, from the disk as it shipped.

sections.h: What you are actually playing
sections.html:
You are in a dungeon of twenty-six levels looking for the Amulet of Yendor, which is on the bottom. Then you have to carry it back up. Almost nobody does.

Every floor is generated when you arrive, so there is nothing to memorise and no map to look up. Potions and scrolls are unidentified — a potion is "a blue potion" until you drink one, and it might heal you or blind you. Monsters are lettered in the original and drawn here, and they get worse as you descend: the kestrel on level two is a nuisance, and the dragon on level twenty is not.

Death is permanent. There is no reloading a good save, because the save is deleted when you resume it. That rule is the reason the genre exists, and it is the reason a run feels like it matters.

sections.h: Why this version looks different
sections.html:
Rogue was written for terminals, so it was made of letters: @ was you, Z was a zombie, and a room was drawn in dashes and pipes. That constraint became the genre's signature, and plenty of modern roguelikes still choose it deliberately.

A.I. Design ported Rogue to the IBM PC and then the Macintosh for Epyx, and on a Mac in 1985 you had a bitmapped screen and a mouse, so they used them. The monsters are little drawings. It is the same game underneath — same generator, same identification puzzle, same permadeath — wearing the only interface the Macintosh had.

It is also a small piece of history in its own right: one of the earliest examples of a text-only game being rebuilt around a graphical interface rather than simply given a font.

sections.html:
Each topic offers the same four ways in. Look and Learn shows worked examples. Build-a-Problem has you assemble the problem rather than only answer it, which catches the children who can compute but cannot read a question. Solve the Problem is straight drill against the clock.

And then Math Blaster, which is the arcade game: answers drift past on a rocket, you fly to the right one and fire. It is not sophisticated — it is a shooting gallery with sums in it — but it is the part every ten-year-old played for, and the part that made the drill tolerable.

The design underneath is the interesting bit. The game does not make the maths easier when you struggle; it makes the presentation change. That was an unusual idea in 1986 and it is the reason the series lasted.

sections.h: Where this came from

Jan Davidson taught, tutored, and in 1982 started writing software on an Apple II at her kitchen table. She and her husband Bob sold the early programs themselves, mailing disks out of the house. Math Blaster was the one that broke through.

By the early 1990s Davidson & Associates was one of the largest educational software publishers in the United States, and it was sold in 1996 for around a billion dollars. Reading Blaster, Science Blaster and a long line of sequels followed, and Math Blaster games are still made today.

The 1986 Macintosh original is a much smaller thing than any of them: one screen, six topics, a rocket, and an editor so that a teacher could put in their own problems. It is also, unmistakably, software written by somebody who had actually taught.

faq.q: Is it any good for a child today?

Start with the Aquarium or StagNation scenario, or a random planet. Starting on Earth is the obvious move and the wrong one, because Earth is already finished and there is very little left for you to cause.

sections.h: What you actually do
sections.html:
You are not building anything. You are turning dials on a planetary model and watching what it does over geological time.

The dials are real ones: continental drift speed, solar input, atmospheric composition, the rate at which life mutates. Raise carbon dioxide and the planet warms, ice retreats, and oceans rise over the land your species was living on. Speed up plate tectonics and you get more volcanoes, more mountains, and a great deal more extinction.

Life arrives on its own if the conditions allow it, evolves through the geological ages, and eventually — if you are lucky and patient — develops technology, at which point it starts changing the atmosphere without consulting you. The end state is a civilisation that leaves the planet. Most runs end in a dead rock instead.

sections.h: The game that was really a model
sections.html:
SimEarth was built with James Lovelock, whose Gaia hypothesis argued that the Earth's biosphere and its physical systems regulate each other as a single self-correcting whole. That is the model under the game, and Lovelock consulted on it directly.

It made for a commercially awkward product. There is no opponent, no score worth chasing, and the time scale means a decision you take now shows its consequences several hundred million years later. Reviewers at the time were split between calling it brilliant and calling it a screensaver with menus.

What it does have is the clearest statement of Will Wright's actual interest, which was never cities: he wanted to build systems complicated enough to surprise the person running them. SimEarth is that idea with nothing else in the way.

sections.h: The four games
sections.html:
Sorter puts words on a conveyor and asks the child to sort them by a shared letter, which is the quiet foundation the other three stand on.

Labeller shows an object and a set of words, and the child picks the one that names it.

Word Train is the one everybody remembers: carriages rolling past carrying three-letter words, each of which has to differ from the last by exactly one letter. cat, cot, cog, dog. It is a word ladder, and it is a genuinely elegant piece of teaching disguised as a train.

sections.h: Why this one mattered
sections.html:
The Learning Company was founded in 1980 by Ann McCormick, Leslie Grimm, Teri Perl and Warren Robinett — Robinett being the Atari programmer who had hidden his own name inside Adventure and invented the video game easter egg in the process.

Their argument was that educational software should be built by people who understood how children actually learn, not by programmers adding a quiz to a game. Grimm, who wrote Reader Rabbit, had a doctorate and had taught reading.

It shows. The four games are not four themes on one drill; they attack the same skill from four directions, and the one everyone remembers — the train — is the one that teaches the most. Reader Rabbit sold for twenty years and became the name an entire category was measured against.

You do not choose your pieces. A queue down the side of the screen shows what is coming, and you must place the next one somewhere before you can see past it. That single rule is what turns a simple idea into a real game: you are always building with the wrong piece and planning around the two you can see.

The flow starts after a short delay and never stops. Reach the required length of pipe before it runs out and you go on to the next level, where it starts sooner and moves faster.

sections.h: How to be good at it
sections.html:
Build long, not direct. The target is a length of pipe, not a destination. A tight spiral in a corner scores the same as a sprawl and takes far less space.

Waste pieces deliberately. A piece you cannot use goes somewhere out of the way, not into your path. Placing a bad piece badly is the most common way to lose.

Use the crossover pieces. The one that carries flow in both directions is worth planning around — it lets your pipe cross its own run and is the basis of every long score.

Replacing costs time. You can drop a new piece on an existing one, and the flow keeps moving while you do. It is an emergency measure, not a strategy.

sections.h: Where it came from, and where it went

The Assembly Line, a small British studio, wrote it for the Amiga in 1989 as Pipe Mania. LucasArts published it in the United States as Pipe Dream, which is the name most people know and the name on this build.

It then spread further than almost any puzzle game of its generation, largely by being copied. The pipe-laying minigame that turns up in BioShock, in half the hacking sequences in games since, and in an enormous number of mobile titles is this, more or less unchanged. It became a piece of shared vocabulary rather than a game people remembered buying.

The original is a tighter thing than any of its descendants: no story around it, no reward screen, just a grid, a queue, and water that is already moving.

intro:
In 1986 the Macintosh was an office machine with a small grey screen, and then Dark Castle arrived: a full-screen black-and-white castle drawn like a woodcut, bats that dive at your head, and rats, and a hunchback throwing rocks down a staircase at you.

It looked like nothing else on any computer, and it sounded like nothing else either. It is still the game people name when they argue the Macintosh was a real games machine.

It is hard, and it was meant to be. The controls split between the keyboard and the mouse — you run and jump with your left hand and aim with your right — and that division takes a while to stop feeling wrong. Turn the difficulty down in the Options menu for the first few attempts; the game does not think less of you.

The castle is three doors from the great hall, each leading to a short branch of rooms, and a fourth that opens onto the Black Knight at the end.

sections.h: Why it looked like that
sections.html:
Mark Stephen Pierce drew it, and he drew it as though the one-bit screen were an engraving rather than a limitation. Everything is cross-hatched, stippled and heavy-lined, and the result has more depth than most colour games of the same year.

The sound is the other half. Dark Castle used digitised audio at a time when nearly every game used beeps — the bats screech, the rocks knock, and your character makes a genuinely upsetting noise when he falls. Silicon Beach recorded that material and shipped it, which is why the game took two floppies when most took one.

The programmer was Jonathan Gay, who was still in his teens. He went on to write the animation tool that became Macromedia Flash, so a reasonable share of the web's first decade traces back to the person who made these bats fly.

sections.h: Getting anywhere
sections.html:
Throw while moving. Standing still to aim is how you get hit. The mouse aims independently of which way you are running, which is the whole point of the control scheme.

Crouch under things. S drops you low, and a great deal of what is thrown at you passes over a crouching character.

Rocks are limited. You carry a finite number and you will run out. Picking up more is often the real objective of a room.

The Trouble door first. Of the three branches it is the gentlest, and it teaches the movement without the rooms that punish it.

faq.q: Is this the original Dark Castle?
faq.a: Yes — version 1.2 of the 1986 Macintosh release, in black and white, as it shipped. Not Return to Dark Castle and not any of the later console conversions, which look and play quite differently.

faq.q: Why are the controls split between mouse and keyboard?
faq.a: Because you aim and move independently. The left hand runs, jumps and crouches; the right hand aims and throws. It is awkward for an hour and then it is the reason the game works.
Turn the difficulty down in the Options menu, and start with the Trouble door. The game was designed for people who would play it for weeks.
Yes, and in 1986 that was remarkable. It is most of why the game shipped on two disks and most of why people remember it.
Silicon Beach Software. Mark Stephen Pierce did the art, Jonathan Gay wrote the code — Gay later created the tool that became Macromedia Flash.

intro:
Gather the crystals, then fly to the exit. Do it while an increasing number of things that want to kill you fill the screen and learn your habits. There is no more to it than that, and Crystal Quest was one of the most-played Macintosh games ever released.

It is controlled entirely with the mouse, which sounds like a compromise and is in fact the reason it feels so good.

Each wave drops a field of crystals and a set of enemies. Collect every crystal and the gate at the edge of the screen opens; fly through it and the next wave starts, harder.

The mouse control is absolute rather than relative — the ship is where the pointer is — so you can cross the screen instantly if your hand can move that fast. That is the skill ceiling, and it is high.

sections.h: The nasties
sections.html:
Enemies arrive by type and each behaves differently, which is the whole strategic layer. Some drift. Some home in. Some sit still and shoot. Some split when you kill them, and killing them at the wrong moment is worse than leaving them alone.

Mines are the ones that get you. They do not chase — they simply sit in the path between you and the last crystal, and the game is very good at placing them where you were about to go.

There is a bonus for finishing a wave quickly and a bigger one for not firing at all, which turns some waves into a pure evasion puzzle. Playing for score and playing to survive are genuinely different games.

sections.h: The voices
sections.html:
Crystal Quest talks. It congratulates you, it insults you when you die, and the sampled voices — recorded by the developers, including a deadpan "ooooh" and a resigned "that's nice" — are the thing every person who played it remembers first.

Patrick Buckland wrote the game; Casady & Greene, a Mac-only publisher with an unusually good ear for what the platform's users wanted, published it. Buckland later founded Rockstar Leeds. Casady & Greene closed in 2003, a Macintosh software house that outlived nearly all the others and is now mostly remembered for this and for Conflict Catcher.

The sound files are still on the disk with their copyright notices in the filenames, which is a small and rather charming piece of 1994 housekeeping.

faq.q: Is this the original Crystal Quest?
faq.a: It is version 2.2.5, the Macintosh release by Casady & Greene. Not the 2007 Xbox Live Arcade remake, which is a different program by different people.
With the mouse alone. The ship goes exactly where you point, and the button fires in whatever direction you are moving.

faq.q: Why can I not use the keyboard?
faq.a: The game was designed around the mouse, and the absolute positioning is the point — you can cross the screen as fast as your hand moves, which no keyboard would allow.
Finish waves quickly, and finish them without firing where you can. The no-shot bonus is large enough that some waves are best played as pure evasion.
Yes. The sampled voices are the first thing most people remember about it, and the sound files are still sitting on the disk with their 1994 copyright notices in the filenames.
